#4789. Helping Your Child Navigate Emotions When You're Overwhelmed

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

We’ve all been there. Your 4-year-old can only find one of their spaceman boots and is in total meltdown; your middle schooler begs not to go to school because they’re convinced they have no one to sit with at lunch; your teen has stormed off when you simply asked if they started their homework. Meanwhile, you are just trying to make it through the finish line of the day. Somehow, it’s not looking good.

Our overwhelm meets their distress. It’s a stressful emotional gridlock.

Our overwhelm often comes from feeling like we have to change course: Do an abrupt swerve to stop or fix what our kids are feeling. And of course, it’s not like our kids don’t want that, but it’s not like that’s all they want either. Witness how, when we make a beeline for solutions, kids often respond with: “You don’t understand! You’re just trying to fix it! You never listen to me!”

But rather than whisking them away from their feelings, our best move is to go toward their emotions with them.

What is the best way for kids to process their emotions? I have created a process I call the Seven Shifts, and it works for any age—parents and kids alike.

The Seven Shifts is a repeatable throughline for any emotional situation; it involves first honoring what you’re feeling so you can settle back into a more thoughtful (versus reactive) state, then toggling to what the feeling is pointing to: the need for us to do our good work—zoom in and understand what our thoughts are telling us, then zoom out to question interpretations and consider other possibilities that are more helpful and… true.

Shift 1: Empathize—don’t fight or fix the feeling; just make room for it

Notice how just saying to yourself: “I’m worried for my child, or even I’m frustrated and too tired, and that’s OK” allows your body to soften. You’re not fighting where you are. You aren’t saying you don’t care; your caring is not up for debate. You are validating your own experience—it’s a place where people land. Lots of people.

Same for your child: Instead of rushing to reassure or correct—get to what I call the “nodding head of agreement.” Your child sees that you see where they are: “This is really upsetting you. This is a lot you’re carrying. You really didn’t want it to be like this.” It’s not about agreeing with the logic; it’s accepting without judgment—this is where your child has landed.

Often in a blur of competing feelings, we feel lost—and when we feel lost, we spiral. The antidote? Just start naming the feelings—there may be several, and they may seem like opposites—like loving and frustrated. They are what I call “Emotion Neighbors”—opposites can sit side by side and not add up: feeling frustrated and sad, hopeful and exhausted.

Kids may not be able to name their feelings—ask: Does it feel mad, like something isn’t OK with you, or more hurt, like something is missing?

Shift 3: Settle inside—slow down and reset

The body registers all the stress of our thoughts. Tiny resets, a big exhale, a sigh, help you shift out of crisis mode and into connection. Bringing your calm to your child helps them find their calm, too. Sometimes it’s invisible—just your slow breathing helps them find their calm. A regulated nervous system is the foundation of everything that follows.

What are the thoughts underneath the feelings? When we can find those gems—not necessarily positive—they tell us what we’ve been telling ourselves; knowing the narrative we’re reading helps point to what we need to reinterpret. When thoughts operate freely under our awareness, we get stuck in spirals of fear, frustration, or helplessness. Ask your child: “What’s your brain telling you? What is the alarm, going beep-beep-beep, in your mind?”

Shift 5: Zoom out—prism it to see multiple perspectives

Now that we’ve unearthed those gems, hold them up to the light and get different perspectives—translation: the things we say to ourselves unchecked we’d never say to a friend in a similar situation. We can fact-check our beliefs and edit accordingly and encourage our kids to do the same.

Help kids get in the habit of what I call “second-opinion thinking”: What would they tell a friend in that situation? What would a friend tell them? What would a hero or mentor say? Notice you’re not saying: “You’re thinking the wrong thing.” It’s an invitation: “Those thoughts sound like what anxiety says; can we fact-check it and see what else is more true?”

Shift 6: Take action one small step at a time

Equipped with a newer, truer story, is there a step you want to take that could help—like allowing yourself a “time out” and coming back to your child when you’ve had a second to reset? Or reminding yourself of your child’s strengths rather than just focusing on what’s wrong?

With your child, ask: “What’s a step that you could try—approaching a fearful situation? Saying something assertive to a friend? Scheduling grief time every day?”

Shift 7: Take stock and give credit where it is due!

We are the heroes of our lives, and our successes are in the tiny moments—notice them, and give credit where credit is due. Help them notice the progress they are making—and the way they made it—especially when things are hard. That’s how they will know how to value the steps along the way, not just the great moments across the finish line.

When we allow ourselves to turn toward—not away—from our emotions, the seven shifts become a two-for-one route toward understanding. Kids gradually learn the way from our responses and increasingly trust that they’ll come out with a better understanding of themselves and the world on the other side of the journey.

Here’s to better emotional navigation all around.

#4787. Electric trucks hit 50% of China’s heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls

Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.

December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.

Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.

That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.

It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.

CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.

Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.

CATL is already taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy.

The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.

For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.

Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.

So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.

China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.

2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.

Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.

There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.

Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.

A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.

The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE, which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.

Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.

This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.

Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.

And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.

The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.

China having a lot of phev and EV vehicles has helped with oil pricing around the world, more notably in the current american-caused oil crisis. It would be worse if they were all traditional powered cars and trucks.

Now to be clear, I'm not saying that it has made a massive impact or is even the only reason why the oil crisis isn't much worse, it's just one of a few steps China made to reduce the impact of the oil crisis. But going electric everywhere we can has a stabilizing effect when oil shocks show up

Europe at least has the regulation, and its best markets, at 10% to 24%, are roughly where China was in 2024 and 2025.

The question now is how long Chinese truck makers stay home. SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them. If those trucks can come close to China’s pricing, how long can Western truck makers keep charging 2x diesel?

Diesel trucks aren’t the only thing batteries are displacing. At home, pairing solar with an EV or a home battery can cut your energy bills dramatically. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4786. PMOS, Formerly PCOS, May Be Associated with Alzheimer's Disease Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), has been linked to changes in brain function and cognition that may overlap with those seen in Alzheimer’s disease.

However, a review published October 13 in the Journal of the Endocrine Society suggests that metabolic conditions commonly associated with PMOS, rather than PMOS itself, may help explain a potential link to Alzheimer’s disease and dementia risk.

“Researchers are exploring whether some metabolic conditions commonly seen in women with PMOS, such as insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, [and] elevated cholesterol, could play a role in dementia, since these are already known risk factors for cognitive decline,” Yesika Garcia, MD, board certified endocrinologist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline.

“In other words, any potential connection may be related to these underlying metabolic issues rather than PMOS itself. I think it’s important to clarify that an association does not mean causation,” she added.

The researchers searched PubMed for studies published through 2025 examining brain structure and function, cognitive performance, biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, and dementia risk in people with PMOS.

Because PMOS is a newer term, the researchers searched for studies using both PMOS and PCOS.

The review identified studies suggesting that people with PMOS may experience mild differences in certain cognitive abilities, including:

Some brain imaging studies using MRI and PET scans identified differences in brain structure and function among people with PMOS. Researchers also observed hormonal changes associated with differences in gray matter.

Some studies identified elevated biomarkers associated with Alzheimer’s disease in people with PMOS. These findings appeared to overlap with metabolic changes seen in type 2 diabetes, particularly those associated with obesity and insulin resistance.

The researchers also found that neurological differences were less pronounced when people with PMOS were compared with metabolically healthy control groups, suggesting that associated metabolic conditions may play an important role in these findings.

Overall, the review suggests that metabolic conditions associated with PMOS may contribute to changes in brain health, although more research is needed to determine whether PMOS independently affects Alzheimer’s disease or dementia risk.

“I think we need to be careful about drawing conclusions too early. The research raises some good questions, but it doesn’t prove that PCOS [PMOS] causes Alzheimer’s disease,” said Dung Trinh, MD, internist, of MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“What it does reinforce is how important metabolic health may be when it comes to protecting our brains as we get older,” he added.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed. She also added that more attention and research need to be given to PMOS, brain changes, and future risks of dementia.

There are various ways that PMOS and dementia may share pathways and overlap, according to the researchers. Some of these shared pathways include:

Trinh explained that insulin resistance may be one of the most important connections between PMOS and dementia.

Although insulin is commonly associated with diabetes and blood sugar regulation, it also plays an important role in brain function. When insulin signaling doesn’t work properly, it may interfere with how brain cells use energy, potentially contributing to problems with memory and thinking over time.

Chronic inflammation, which can occur in people with PMOS, may also play a role in Alzheimer’s disease, Trinh told Healthline.

“Researchers are looking at how these metabolic changes may affect amyloid and tau, two proteins associated with Alzheimer’s. Some brain imaging studies have even found differences in brain structure and function among women with PCOS [PMOS],” he said.

Ross added that elevated androgen levels, which are common in people with PMOS, may also play a role in dementia risk.

“An important distinction is that these risk factors are not present in every woman with PMOS, and having PMOS does not automatically mean someone will experience cognitive decline,” cautioned Garcia.

Garcia noted that many of the dementia risk factors associated with PMOS are modifiable.

“Regular exercise, including both cardiovascular activity and strength training, can improve insulin sensitivity, help with weight management, and support cardiovascular and brain health,” she added.

“A Mediterranean-style diet, with plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean sources of protein, is a reasonable place to start,” he said.

Managing blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure is also important, Trinh and Garcia noted.

“Medication, like metformin, can also improve insulin resistance, which may further reduce the risk of dementia,” Ross added.

Getting adequate sleep, avoiding smoking, and staying mentally and socially active are additional ways to support long-term brain health, Garcia told Healthline.

“For someone with PCOS [PMOS], I would encourage regular visits with their healthcare provider to monitor metabolic health and address problems early,” said Trinh.

“While we cannot say that these interventions specifically prevent dementia in women with PMOS, we know they benefit overall metabolic and cardiovascular health, which are closely connected to brain health,” explained Garcia.

#4785. Lexus is taking a page from China for its next electric SUV launching in 2027

Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus is launching a new electric SUV in 2027, its first vehicle built in China in over two decades.

It’s official. Toyota is breaking from tradition, planning to develop and produce the new vehicle in China rather than its home market of Japan.

Lexus confirmed the new vehicle will be made at its new manufacturing plant in Jinshan, Shanghai, and will go on sale in 2027.

As the first Lexus factory built from scratch overseas, the company said the new plant will bring together its global manufacturing capabilities.

Toyota broke ground on the facility in June 2025, saying the new facility will unlock “Lexus speed” as it aims to keep pace with domestic brands like BYD. Construction was expected to be completed this past August, with the first vehicle scheduled to roll off the assembly line in the fall of 2027.

The first Lexus model will be an electric SUV, produced using advanced manufacturing methods such as gigacasting to reduce costs and speed up output.

The facility will be a cornerstone of Toyota’s comeback plans in China, where it’s struggled to compete with local brands.

Production capacity will be around 1,000 units per month in 2027 as Toyota ramps up to “tens of thousands” in 2028.

Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20% in China last month, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales than the year prior. The market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” Toyota said.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Lexus’ new Shanghai facility is wholly owned by Toyota, enabling it to produce vehicles in China through its joint ventures.

The new electric SUV will go on sale in China in 2027. Specific details, including battery, range, and prices, have yet to be announced.

As part of its “with China, for China, strategy, Lexus said it will “continue to use China as a source of innovation,” adding it will “deepen localization efforts” to bring classic models to the market that meet local needs.

Toyota joins the growing list of major OEMs that are already tapping, or plan to tap, China for its next-generation electric vehicles.

While in other global markets, Toyota is sticking to its “multi-pathway” strategy, which includes all powertrains from electric to ICE; in China, it’s being forced to adapt.

China is Toyota’s third-largest market, following the US and Japan. To stay competitive and turn things around in China, Toyota will rely more on local partners and suppliers.

Developing the new Lexus electric SUV in China first rather than Japan is significant given Toyota’s traditional ways.

Typically, it takes Toyota about four to five years to fully develop a new vehicle. In China, automakers are now building them in as little as two years.

Toyota, like many automakers at this point, is turning to China for new tech, batteries, production methods, and other EV components to keep pace.

#4784. How Cerebro-Cerebellar Loop Fluidity Drives Sports Mastery

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Back in the early 2000s, when I was deeply immersed in ultra-endurance running and writing about the brain mechanics of peak performance, my working theory of motor expertise was straightforward, if a bit reductionist.

Based on late-20th-century motor learning paradigms like the Marr-Albus framework, I believed that achieving athletic success was primarily about "hammering and forging" cerebellar Purkinje cells through thousands of hours of repetitive practice.

The ultimate goal, as I saw it then, was to offload complex coordinated movement patterns entirely to the cerebellum, bypass the cerebral cortex's overthinking trap, and avoid choking due to "paralysis by analysis."

For a long time, this compartmentalized view felt intuitively correct. When a tennis player serves an ace or a baseball slugger hits a 100-mph fastball over the fence, it looks and feels automatic. We assumed the cerebral cortex simply stepped out of the way once a skill became hardwired in the cerebellum.

However, science moves forward. Over the past decade, neuroimaging and systems neuroscience have revealed that motor expertise is far less about segregating brain regions and much more about how seamlessly they communicate.

As I've noted previously when exploring cerebro-cerebellar circuits, knowing how to perform a movement mentally is never enough; the essence of sports mastery lies in the bidirectional, closed-loop dialogue connecting the cerebrum and the cerebellum.

Now, a first-of-its-kind multimodal neuroimaging study (Filip et al., 2026) published in The Cerebellum provides empirical evidence that redefines our understanding of this neural architecture once again.

To understand how elite motor timing works, the research team compared 41 expert baseball and softball players—representing a natural human model of optimized motor timing—against 46 nonathletic controls. Using a sophisticated framework combining task-based functional MRI (fMRI) with quantitative advanced MRI techniques like neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) and adiabatic T1ρ mapping, the researchers uncovered a fascinating paradox.

When performing predictive timing tasks, nonathletic controls engaged a widespread, energy-intensive network across sensorimotor, visuospatial, attentional, and frontoparietal systems seated in the cerebrum.

By contrast, the athletic experts exhibited attenuated task engagement, meaning their brains ran the predictive control program with significantly less overall neural effort. They weren't brute-forcing the motion or taxing the cerebral real estate responsible for conscious strategy and spatial awareness. Instead, by delegating the rapid rhythm of the movement to the cerebellum, experts achieved a seamless partnership between the two regions, optimizing whole-brain neural efficiency.

Notably, lower baseline engagement didn't mean elite-level athletes were sleepwalking through the task.

While their baseline neural effort dropped, the expert hitters displayed enhanced error-related modulation. When a microscopic deviation occurred, their neural systems registered the error with exquisite sensitivity.

This bridges the gap between what I got right and what I missed in my early-2000s assumptions. I was right to suspect that pro athletes run motor programs efficiently without clogging up working memory with cumbersome, conscious commands. However, I was wrong to view the cerebral cortex and cerebellum as operating in total isolation or taking turns.

Instead of a split-brain dichotomy between the cerebrum and cerebellum, peak performance relies on cerebro-cerebellar loop fluidity.

Once an athlete lays down this robust, dual-brain circuitry through deliberate practice, the network operates with remarkable metabolic and functional efficiency. But the moment a fraction of a millisecond is off in a swing or a stroke, the frontoparietal and cerebellar loops instantly catch the micro-error, allowing the athlete to subconsciously fine-tune their mechanics on the fly.

The researchers also evaluated underlying tissue properties using NODDI and T1ρ (T1-rho) mapping. While in vivo MRI cannot isolate individual neurons, these metrics capture microscopic changes driven heavily by the sprawling dendritic arbors of Purkinje cells and dense granule cell packing.

The findings showed that distributed cortical networks in experts exhibited higher neurite density, while the cerebellum displayed a specialized profile characterized by higher neurite density, lower orientation dispersion, and faster T1ρ relaxation times.

While the term "relaxation" might sound like it is referencing a psychological state of calm, in MRI physics, relaxation quantifies how quickly magnetic signals return to baseline, which happens faster in denser, highly organized cellular environments.

That said, this linguistic coincidence beautifully mirrors an athlete's lived experience: Faster T1ρ relaxation times actually help facilitate psychological relaxation on the playing field. Because the cerebellar hardware is so densely woven and metabolically efficient, an athlete stepping up to bat or serving a tennis ball doesn't need to rely on anxious, cortical overthinking. Ultimately, the physical density of the brain tissue enables a mental state of calm, hyper-focused flow.

These structural fingerprints indicate that decades of physical training physically alter the tissue architecture, optimizing the brain's ability to process rapid timing signals and coordinate feedforward control.

As an athlete turned science writer, looking back at my early writing on cerebellar function in motor expertise, I realize that I may have been a bit overzealous in attributing elite performance to turning off cerebral thinking and letting the cerebellum completely take over.

The new reality unearthed by Filip et al. (2026) doesn't discard the cerebellum's role, but it highlights that athletic perfection isn't about silencing the cortex or surrendering entirely to the cerebellum. It's about forging a hyper-efficient, highly responsive network where cerebral strategy and cerebellar timing merge into a single, fluid loop—one that stays quiet until a micro-adjustment is needed to turn a near-miss into a home run.

Pavel Filip, Lenka Marková, Cecile Gallea, Stéphane Lehéricy, Ovidiu V. Lungu, Shalom Michaeli, Silvia Mangia, Viktor Weiss, Martin Bareš & Lubomír Vojtíšek. "Motor Expertise Combines Lower Task Engagement With Enhanced Error Sensitivity." The Cerebellum (First published: November 04, 2026)

David Marr. "A Theory of Cerebellar Cortex." The Journal of Physiology (First published: June 01, 1969) doi:10.1113/jphysiol.1969.sp008820

James S. Albus. "A Theory of Cerebellar Function." Mathematical Biosciences (First published: February 01, 1971) doi:10.1016/0025-5564(71)90051-4

#4783. I Work Out for a Living—Here Are the Best Headphones for Everything From Runs to Gym Sessions

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Because every sweat session needs an epic soundtrack.

WHETHER YOU PREFER to listen to music, a podcast, or tune into sports while getting your sweat on, you'll need a solid pair of workout headphones to make it happen. Beyond a high-quality pre-workout, nothing elevates your training quite like the perfect pair of headphones. These devices not only drown out grunting gym-goers but also help you stay focused, find your rhythm, and push through those last few reps when your body is telling you to quit.

The key to a good pair of workout headphones is finding ones that fit your ears snugly and won't budge while you run or do kettlebell swings. Workout headphones need water resistance to handle sweat and 5-mile runs in the rain. We can recommend eleven pairs of workout headphones for a range of training environments.

Like our favorite running shoes, modern workout headphones are built for performance, combining durability with athletic-minded features. Sweat and water resistance are non-negotiable, while a secure, comfortable fit prevents them from falling out during burpees, sprints, or heavy lifts. Meanwhile, battery life has improved dramatically in recent years. Many models offer enough juice to power through a week’s worth of workouts on a single charge. Need to focus? Noise cancellation, intuitive controls, and quick-pairing technology keep you in the zone rather than fumbling with your tech.

Whether you’re just starting your fitness journey or a seasoned athlete, the best workout headphones can transform your training sessions. The Men’s Health fitness and tech editors tested a few dozen options to identify the eleven best models available. From true wireless earbuds to over-ear models to bone conduction headphones, these top-performing headphones deliver impressive durability, high-quality sound, and workout-specific features to help you push through the pain.

The AirPods Pro have improved significantly over the past few updates, and the latest version, the AirPods Pro 3, is what we believe are the best do-it-all workout headphones. These earbuds deliver excellent comfort, premium features, and high-quality sound. Apple has systematically addressed every pain point we experienced with earlier models, transforming these wireless earbuds from casual earbuds into essential fitness companions.

The fit is a major reason the AirPods Pro work so well during workouts, even surpassing the latest Apple release, the Apple AirPods 5. After dozens of reps, we found they don’t budge. The multiple silicone ear tips let our testing team find the perfect seal during burpees and box jumps. Despite wearing them for multiple training sessions (and in the office), we experienced no ear fatigue thanks to their lightweight design.

The improved ergonomics also contribute to better passive noise isolation, working with active noise cancellation to block out excessively loud gym music. For athletes who rely on music for motivation during workouts, the secure, comfortable fit eliminates the constant annoyance of loose earbuds that need readjusting. Their IP57 rating provides additional peace of mind, ensuring they can handle the sweat that comes with serious workouts.

MH Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM, found the most exciting new feature of the AirPods Pro 3s to be their ability to monitor your heart rate through your ear canals, a capability more commonly associated with devices that wrap around your wrist or chest. They aren't the first headphones to do so, but having this added to Apple's already impressive offerings only strengthens their case.

Battery life exceeded our expectations, with up to eight hours of continuous playback and a charging case that extends total listening time to 24 hours. The case supports wireless charging, making it easy to recharge on a charging pad. Meanwhile, the AirPods Pro 3 support several advanced features like adaptive audio, conversation awareness, and transparency mode, the latter of which lets outside sound in, so you can be aware of what’s going on around you during a run.

The touch controls are intuitive during workouts—you can play/pause, skip tracks, answer a call, and adjust the volume by pressing the stem. For iPhone owners, the AirPods are a cinch to set up. Simply open the case next to your phone, tap Connect, and you’re ready to go. This combination of comfort, performance, and ease of use makes the AirPods Pro 3 the best overall workout headphones, setting a high bar for others to match.

Read More: Our Review of the Apple AirPods Pro 3s

While the Beats Studio Pro aren’t specifically designed for working out, they’re by no means out of place in a gym. The headphones maintain the sleek, recognizable Beats aesthetic and bass-heavy sound the brand is known for, while offering premium features that make them great for training and office use.

The over-ear design provides top-notch sound isolation through plush memory foam ear cushions, while the adjustable headband distributes weight evenly across your head. They balance comfort with stability—the headband applies just enough pressure to keep the headphones secure without becoming uncomfortable during extended wear. During testing, the Studio Pro remained firmly in place through moderate workouts like weightlifting and walks, though they’re not ideal for high-impact exercises.

Battery life is fantastic, lasting up to 40 hours with ANC off (24 hours with ANC on). When the battery gets low, you can get up to 4 hours of playback with just 10 minutes of USB-C charging. The Studio Pro offers excellent cross-OS compatibility, including quick pairing and Find My capabilities. However, features like spatial audio and dynamic head tracking are exclusive to iPhone owners.

That said, the Studio Pro omits some features that are standard on other premium models, like ear detection, so they don’t automatically pause the music when you remove them from your head. Still, the headphones provide impressive performance wrapped in the brand’s iconic style.

Read More: Best Workout Clothes For Men, Tested by Us

The Powerbeats Pro 2 by Beats are a fresh addition to the workout headphone market and have quickly become our top choice among models with ear hooks. Nearly six years after the original, Beats has introduced major upgrades like active noise cancellation, transparency mode, and heart rate monitoring—a feature typically found in smartwatches. Setting up these headphones was a breeze, with the same seamless iPhone connectivity you’d expect from AirPods.

We prefer the fit and look of the Powerbeats Pro 2 compared to the first generation. The previous model’s ear hooks felt awkward, but the new design is much more comfortable, with five different ear tip sizes for a secure fit. During testing, these headphones felt glued to our ears—even during a windy run—and didn’t flinch after getting drenched in sweat thanks to the IPX4 rating. The softer plastic avoids the slimy feel after intense workouts, allowing them to transition quickly from the gym to the office.

In addition to a comfortable fit, the sound quality has improved significantly, with balanced bass that enhances the listening experience without overpowering it. We appreciated the intuitive controls, with a button on each earbud for volume control—clicking the right to increase and the left to decrease. Pausing and skipping tracks was also easy by tapping the sides of each earbud. Making calls was straightforward, with excellent sound quality, and the battery percentage displayed more precisely on our phone than other headphones, which often rounded to the nearest 10 percent.

Each earbud features a built-in sensor—the same tech found in the Apple Watch—for heart rate monitoring. It’s a nice feature, providing valuable insights into your performance during workouts. However, if you already own an Apple Watch, this feature might feel redundant.

While there’s a lot to like about the Powerbeats Pro 2, the side buttons can be overly sensitive. During runs, we occasionally found ourselves accidentally pausing or skipping tracks while adjusting the fit or changing the volume. If you own an iPhone, you’ll get the most value from these earbuds, benefiting from features like dynamic head tracking, automatic device switching, and Find My integration. However, Android users can still enjoy the earbuds with one-touch pairing, customizable controls, and the Locate My Beats feature available through the Beats app.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 holds the top spot among the best bone conduction headphones and was featured in the 2025 Men’s Health Tech Awards, so it’s no surprise they’re a favorite here.

The classic wraparound design and open-ear style are incredibly comfortable, particularly during longer runs. The lightweight titanium frame rests against your temples rather than in your ear canals, eliminating the discomfort and ear fatigue you might experience with traditional earbuds. The design feels funky at first, but once you get used to it, you’ll appreciate not having anything in your ears.

After testing the OpenRun Pro 2 on both long and short runs, we found the design goes beyond comfort. Perhaps the most significant advantage is the enhanced safety it provides. Unlike traditional earbuds that can block external sounds, these headphones leave your ear canals completely unobstructed, so you stay fully aware of your surroundings. This is crucial for runners who need to hear approaching vehicles and other hazards.

Despite the open-ear design, the OpenRun Pro 2 produces high-quality sound. Shokz’s DualPitch tech helps eliminate unwanted vibrations, so audio comes through clearly—something bone conduction headphones struggle with. Even in noisy environments like busy streets or gyms, we didn’t have to max out the volume to hear our favorite tunes. In addition to its lightweight design, the headphones offer up to 12 hours of battery life and an IP55 rating, so they’ll hold up to your toughest workouts.

The Bose Ultra Open earbuds depart from traditional in-ear designs, with a clip-on style that rests against your ear rather than inside it. This unconventional approach keeps you aware of your surroundings while still delivering premium features and sound quality. For runners or cyclists, they’re a compelling alternative to conventional earbuds and bone conduction headphones.

Setup is straightforward, with quick pairing with both Android and iOS devices, and a Bose Music app that lets you customize EQ settings and update the firmware. While the design takes some getting used to, particularly getting them just right on your ear, the lightweight design is comfortable, with little to no ear fatigue. We worried the clip-on style would slip during quick head movements, but they stayed secure and never jostled loose.

Sound quality is impressive considering the open design, with Bose’s OpenAudio technology directing sound toward your ears. They don’t match the experience of noise-canceling earbuds, but the audio performance strikes an impressive balance for anyone who needs to remain aware of their surroundings. Meanwhile, the dual-microphone array delivers excellent call quality, even in noisy environments.

Battery life is about 9 hours per charge, with the case providing an additional 19.5 hours. IPX4 water resistance protects against sweat and light rain, making these suitable for most outdoor activities. For users who find traditional earbuds uncomfortable, the Bose Ultra Open is a refreshing alternative while delivering the quality we’ve come to expect from the brand.

At $30, the JLab Go Sport+ is the perfect entry-level option for runners. The flexible earhooks keep the buds locked in place, the sound is decent enough to keep you moving, and an IP55 rating means sweat isn’t a concern. Be Aware mode lets ambient sound in when you need it, and the JLab app offers EQ presets if you want to tweak the sound.

Battery life is another standout, reaching up to 9 hours on a single charge and extending to 35 hours with a case that conveniently includes a built-in USB-C cable. If you just need something reliable that won’t sting to replace when they inevitably go missing, these are it.

The Pixel Buds Pro 2 are the earbuds to get if you own a Pixel phone, offering an integration experience that rivals the seamless connection between AirPods and iPhones. Google’s second-generation earbuds build on their predecessor with improved ANC, a more comfortable design, and enhanced sound quality, making them an easy choice for Google users.

The silicone ear tips create a secure seal, while a small “stabilizer” (basically a tiny fin) on each earbud helps them stay in place when you’re moving around. With an IPX4 rating, the Buds Pro 2 handle sweat without issue, so you can use them on a rainy-day run. The matte finish on both the buds and the case resists fingerprints and maintains a premium feel even after extended use.

Sound quality has been upgraded thanks to new 11mm dynamic drivers. Google’s spatial audio delivers an immersive listening experience for compatible content, while the Tensor-powered adaptive EQ automatically adjusts to your environment. The improved noise cancellation is particularly impressive, effectively blocking noise. Touch controls on each earbud are responsive without being overly sensitive, and the conversation detection feature automatically pauses music when you start speaking.

Battery life is around eight hours with ANC enabled, with the case providing an additional 30 hours. A quick five-minute charge delivers about one-and-a-half hours of listening time in a pinch. Overall, the Buds Pro 2 are the best wireless earbuds for Pixel phone owners, offering excellent comfort, sound quality, and durability. Plus, you get powerful features like Live Translate and Gemini support, making them more than just workout headphones.

Android users have no shortage of options, including those on this list. But Samsung’s extremely lightweight Galaxy Buds 3 Pro stand out, offering excellent features and performance for everyday use and workouts. Their AirPods-like stem design is more comfortable and secure than the Buds 2 Pro, with silicone ear tips (available in 3 sizes) that create an effective seal without causing discomfort during extended wear. They’ll stay firmly in place through running, HIIT workouts, and strength training sessions.

The IP57 rating provides excellent protection against both dust and water, making these earbuds capable of surviving temporary submersion up to 1 meter. If you like to rough it while working out, these earbuds are durable enough. The Galaxy Buds 3 Pro earbuds also deliver high-quality sound, with an adaptive mode that blends ANC based on your surroundings. These features work seamlessly, so you can hear important sound cues like sirens more easily.

Powerful voice controls elevate the hands-free experience, letting you manage playback, adjust volume, and toggle between listening modes without a specific wake phrase—simply say “volume up,” and the earbuds will increase the volume. While these earbuds get just about everything right, they lack true multipoint connectivity, meaning they can’t maintain simultaneous active connections to multiple devices. However, Samsung users benefit from Auto Switch technology, which automatically transitions the earbuds between your Galaxy phone, tablet, and laptop whenever you start media on a different device.

For people whose ears tend to reject standard earbuds, the Powerbeats Fit offer a secure alternative with its flexible wingtips and snug, workout-friendly design. While the unusual fit takes some getting used to, our testing found the buds stayed put during HIIT, running, strength training, and everyday use.

"They're still the finest, and steadiest fitness earbuds out there," says Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. "The latest iteration doesn't change too much of the (very effective) formula they've had, which is just fine because they work so well."

Fit can vary by ear shape, and one of our testers initially experienced soreness from the wingtips—an issue that eased with shorter wear times and a switch to smaller ear tips. Once adjusted, the seal improved both comfort and sound quality. The wingtips effectively prevent slippage during intense workouts, though you need to place them carefully to keep them secure.

Sound quality is strong for workout earbuds, with active noise cancellation and transparency modes that are easy to toggle in the app, though not quite as robust as the AirPods Pro. Controls are simple, with identical tap functions on each side, plus handy features like auto-pause and magnetic charging-case guidance. The 30-hour battery life is a major advantage.

We were a little bummed that the box doesn't include a USB-C charging cable or on-earbud volume control. While other headphones with ear hooks may feel even more secure, the Powerbeats Fit offers a compelling blend of stability, sound, and battery life. At $200, they’re a worthwhile pick for anyone who needs earbuds that reliably stay put during tough workouts.

Read More: Our Full Review of the Powerbeats Fit

Open earbuds let outside noise in by design, but that same openness can make it hard to hear your audio on a busy street. The Shokz OpenFit Pro tackles this with a triple-microphone array and adaptive algorithm that dampens outside noise without sealing your ear canal. It won’t replace full ANC, but it quiets things just enough that you can actually enjoy what you’re listening to. Sound quality has also improved over previous OpenFit models, with better bass response and zero distortion at higher volumes.

The soft silicone ear hooks sit behind your ears, keeping the buds stable during runs and listening sessions—and because of the open-ear design, you stay aware of your surroundings the entire time—a real safety advantage over traditional earbuds. Battery life is solid, too, stretching 12 hours without noise reduction and extending to 50 hours total with the case.

JBL has always known how to do bass, and the Endurance Race 2 lives up to that reputation. The 6.8mm dynamic drivers deliver a low-end that’s full and punchy without overpowering the mids, which is exactly what you want when a heavy playlist is the only thing getting you through a final set. JBL’s Twistlock wing design twists into your ear, keeping them in place during jumping exercises.

The IP68 rating means these can handle full submersion, not just sweat. ANC and Smart Ambient mode let you toggle between blocking out the gym and staying aware of traffic on a run. Battery life tops out at 12 hours per charge, with the case extending that to 48 hours total. That’s enough to last a long weekend without needing to find a wall outlet.

If you go hard during your workouts, you'll sweat—probably a lot. You need headphones that can keep up. Look for headphones or earbuds that are at least water-resistant or, even better, waterproof. Really, earbuds usually offer better sweat resistance than over-ear headphones. Over-ear headphones with sweat-resistant construction are a lot harder to find, although brands like Sony and Beats still hold up well to sweat. If most of your workouts are moderate, sweat resistance may not matter, and any pair of the workout headphones we've noted below will work for you.

Your favorite gym clothes aren't the only things drenched in sweat after a workout. So durability for workout headphones starts with water and sweat protection, measured by the standardized Ingress Protection (IP) rating system. The rating has two numbers: the first indicates dust protection (6 being the highest), and the second indicates water resistance (9 being the highest).

For serious athletes (and seriously sweaty workouts), we recommend headphones that offer water protection to survive intense training sessions. If you primarily work out indoors, you can get by without dust protection, but consider proper dust resistance if you’re trail running or doing HIIT on the beach. Beyond dust and water resistance, the best workout headphones boast impact-resistant materials, such as durable plastic, high-grade silicone or rubber, and reinforced hinges and headbands.

Comfort and fit are essential for peak performance. While these factors can be highly personal, certain features separate the headphones you’ll love wearing from those that’ll end up at the bottom of your gym bag.

Several types of workout headphones suit different preferences. In-ear models are the most popular for workouts thanks to their compact size, and they come in several variations. The first type features interchangeable silicone tips in small, medium, and large sizes, creating a customized seal in your ear canal. Another design incorporates flexible ear hooks that loop over your ears for added stability.

If you don’t like wearing earbuds, on-ear headphones provide cushioned pads that rest against your ears, while over-ear models create a complete seal around each ear. Bone conduction headphones offer a unique solution by conducting sound through your cheekbones while keeping your ear canals open. These are a good option for anyone who needs to maintain awareness of their surroundings, such as when running at night or in a busy city.

When you’re crushing a grueling rowing routine or leg day, the last thing you want is your headphones dying mid-workout. Look for wireless earbuds that provide at least six to eight hours of continuous playback, or on-ear/over-ear headphones that can go 20+ hours on a single charge. That should last through a full week of workouts.

The good news is most earbuds come with charging cases that can extend total battery life by several hours; it’s like having a portable battery with you at all times. Additionally, features like wireless charging and fast charging make it even more convenient to keep your headphones powered up, whether you’re dropping them on a charging pad before bed or need a quick boost before heading out the door.

Obtuse controls can throw off your entire rhythm, so look for earbuds and headphones with simple buttons or touch controls. The best workout headphones feature intuitive controls that let you skip tracks, adjust the volume, and answer phone calls—all without touching your phone. Some headphones even offer customizable controls through companion apps, allowing you to tailor the experience to your needs.

Connectivity should be equally seamless. That means pairing quickly with your smartphone without jumping through menus and Bluetooth settings. For instance, the AirPods Pro 3 and Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are easy to pair with an iPhone—simply open the earbuds’ case near your device and tap to connect. Once paired, your AirPods can automatically connect to all your Apple devices through iCloud. Android users can take advantage of Fast Pair technology, which offers a similar one-tap connection experience with compatible headphones.

Additionally, many models now support multipoint pairing, allowing you to seamlessly switch between your phone and computer without manually disconnecting and reconnecting your headphones each time. Voice assistant integration adds another layer of hands-free convenience, letting you control your music, set a timer, or make a phone call using just your voice.

For those of us who work in busy offices, active noise cancellation (ANC) can be a game-changer for blocking out distractions. In gyms, this technology is just as useful, drowning out clanking weights, loud conversations, and blaring music.

However, the best workout headphones don’t just block out noise—they also let noise in. For outdoor workouts (or simply walking down the street), a transparency mode is an essential safety feature that uses the headphones’ microphones to pipe in ambient noise, such as approaching vehicles and emergency sirens. The most effective models let you switch between ANC and transparency modes with a simple tap or voice command.

Beyond noise cancellation, adaptive audio can automatically adjust the sound based on your environment, so you don’t have to constantly fiddle with volume controls.

For the past six years, Men's Health's fitness and tech editors have been testing dozens of the top workout headphones for men. Experts, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM, Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, and Senior Gear Editor Ryan Brower, have put countless options through the paces in multiple workout types to evaluate their fit, durability, comfort, sound quality, and price throughout all of it.

The testing environments included, but weren't limited to, busy CrossFit boxes, elite performance facilities, mountain trails, garage gyms, and outdoor tracks. We even wrote this story while testing various models to listen to podcasts, tunes, and even books in a busy work environment.

The guide below highlights what we believe are the best workout headphones to know about right now.

Sweat causes a lot of wear and tear on over-ear headphones, especially the ear pads. We recommend using only over-ear headphones for moderate activity, such as lifting and light cardio. You don't really want to wear over-ear headphones for HIIT or other high-cardio workouts, because the more sweat you create, the more likely your headphones are to slip and slide around on your head.

Over-ear headphones do provide great sound quality, and if you are strategic about how you work out with them, you likely won't see sweat as an issue until much farther down the road. In one specific case, one of our editors was a big fan of his Beats Studio Pro headphones for weight lifting. It took about 3 years for his ear pads to wear down from sweat and regular use, so he then bought replacement ear pads for those headphones.

You won't have any problems with sweat and water resistance on the running headphones we curated above; however, some are rated higher than others—which means they're more durable.

When you see an "IP" rating, what you are really reading is the Ingress Protection rating. You can read a rating from each number: the first indicates dust protection, and the second indicates water protection. Some of the headphones above have an "X" as the first number. The X indicates that no data were collected on dust protection. Sometimes it helps to know the dust protection, especially if you're running on trails. If you're a trail runner, it's probably worth paying attention to the more rugged running headphones that also have a dust rating.

The second number indicates how waterproof the headphones are. Zero is the lowest, while 9K is the highest (you're unlikely to see a 9K rating on headphones because this level is reserved for materials that can handle direct, high-temp, high-pressure water).

So what's a good number range to look for? We recommend anything between four and six, but seven and higher is a premium rating and can withstand full submersion in water. Most of what you will see is "IPX4", which is solid, but if you're really wanting a pair of running headphones that are made to handle high activity, then look for a second number of seven or above.

#4782. BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter, topping 300,000

BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

#4781. RJ Mitte's Death Highlights Mental Health Challenges for People With Cerebral Palsy

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Breaking Bad” actor and disability advocate RJ Mitte has died at age 34.

Mitte reportedly died by suicide, his representative told People on October 12. However, local authorities have said the official cause and manner of his death remain under investigation.

Mitte, who was best-known for playing Walter White Jr. on the Emmy Award-winning television series “Breaking Bad,” lived with cerebral palsy and advocated for disability inclusion.

There is currently no evidence to suggest that cerebral palsy caused the actor’s death. Still, Mitte’s untimely passing highlights the mental health challenges that people with cerebral palsy may face.

Research has demonstrated elevated risks of anxiety and depression among those with the condition, alongside barriers to diagnosis, social participation, and employment.

“Living with cerebral palsy can affect mental health through several interacting pathways,” said Shannel Elhelou, neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Centric Neuropsychology in Westlake Village, CA.

“Chronic pain, fatigue, disrupted sleep, and the effort required to navigate daily activities can take an emotional toll. Experiences of bullying, discrimination, social exclusion, and difficulty accessing care can add to that burden. Also, the early brain injury underlying cerebral palsy may contribute to difficulties with emotional regulation, although each person’s experience is different,” Elhelou told Healthline.

If you or someone you know is in crisis and considering suicide or self-harm, please seek support:

If you’re calling on behalf of someone else, stay with them until help arrives. You may remove weapons or substances that can cause harm if you can do so safely.

If you’re not in the same household, stay on the phone with them until help arrives.

Mitte played a key role in challenging stereotypes by portraying a teenager with cerebral palsy on “Breaking Bad.”

Outside of acting, Mitte advocated for people with disabilities through organizations including United Cerebral Palsy (UCP) and Shriners Children’s.

He also led the Mitte Foundation, a non-profit corporation founded in 1994 by his grandparents, Roy F. and Joann Cole Mitte, that improves the quality of life for people in Central Texas.

Mitte’s advocacy emphasized representation, inclusion, and opportunities for people with disabilities.

The legacy he leaves behind underscores the need to recognize mental health as an essential part of care for individuals with cerebral palsy and other disabilities.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of conditions affecting movement, posture, and coordination.

Most people with cerebral palsy have typical intelligence, although some also have intellectual disabilities or other comorbid physical and mental health conditions.

A 2018 study published in JAMA Neurology found that adults with cerebral palsy had a 28% higher risk of developing depression and a 40% higher risk of anxiety than adults without the condition.

A 2024 study in JAMA Network Open found higher recorded rates of anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) among children and young adults with cerebral palsy.

The researchers also identified comparatively low rates of depression and suicidal ideation, highlighting concerns that these conditions may be underdiagnosed.

“Research shows that adults with cerebral palsy have an increased risk of depression and anxiety,” Elhelou said.

“However, these conditions should never be viewed as an inevitable part of having a disability. One concern is ‘diagnostic overshadowing,’ when symptoms of depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions are attributed to cerebral palsy itself, leading those conditions to go unrecognized and untreated. Someone’s fatigue, withdrawal, or changes in behavior deserve careful assessment rather than the assumption that ‘this is just their cerebral palsy,'” she continued.

“While these findings help us understand mental health risks among people with cerebral palsy, they cannot tell us what any one person was experiencing. Many interacting factors may contribute to someone dying by suicide, and it would be inappropriate to attribute an individual’s death to their disability.”

A 2019 study published in Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology found that children with cerebral palsy had higher odds of anxiety disorders and behavioral challenges than children without the condition.

Difficulties with friendships and bullying were associated with some of these differences.

Factors that may affect well-being include:

The researchers also found that supportive friendships may help reduce some of these disparities, reinforcing the importance of inclusive schools and communities.

A 2021 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that U.S. adults with disabilities faced increased risks of suicidal thoughts, planning, and attempts compared with adults without disabilities.

The 988 Lifeline received more than 8 million contacts through calls, texts, chats, and American Sign Language videophone in 2025, according to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

Federal funding for the Lifeline’s dedicated LGBTQ+ youth service ended in July 2025, removing the option to press 3 for specialized support.

After pressure from Congress, the service was recently restored at the end of September, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF).

Employment and financial independence can influence well-being for anyone, particularly those with cerebral palsy.

However, a 2024 study found that just 30.4% of young adults with cerebral palsy who participated in vocational rehabilitation programs were employed when they exited those programs.

Workplace accommodations, accessible hiring, vocational rehabilitation, and inclusive social opportunities can help address these barriers.

“Depression and anxiety are treatable, and they should never be dismissed as an inevitable part of living with a disability,” Elhelou said.

“If you notice persistent sadness, anxiety, hopelessness, or withdrawal, reach out to someone you trust and a mental health professional. You deserve a clinician who takes your concerns seriously and adapts treatment to your communication, mobility, or other access needs. Care should also address pain, fatigue, and sleep difficulties, which can affect emotional well-being.”

Organizations such as United Cerebral Palsy offer information and support for people with cerebral palsy and their families.

Healthcare professionals can also improve outcomes by screening for mental health concerns, using appropriate assessment tools, and connecting patients with accessible treatment.

Improved access to care, inclusive communities, and meaningful opportunities can help people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities thrive.

“Asking for help does not diminish your resilience or your contributions. If you are experiencing thoughts of suicide or feel overwhelmed, you do not have to wait until things feel unbearable to reach out,” Elhelou said.

“Supportive relationships, peer groups, and disability communities can offer connection and understanding. Staying engaged in activities that bring enjoyment and meaning can also help.”

#4780. Do Our Choices Reflect Our Values?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

We often hear about the importance of living according to our values. Yet asserting our values is not the same as examining how they shape our decisions. When we lose sight of them or face competing commitments and pressures, we can sometimes fail to act on them. On the other hand, understanding how to incorporate them into our decision-making can help us act on them more consistently.

According to Lilach Sagiv and colleagues, personal values are “broad desirable goals that motivate people’s action and serve as guiding principles in their lives.”

As goals, values are not directed towards specific achievements but rather guide decisions across various aspects of our lives. For example, people who value honesty will try to tell the truth and seek out honest people wherever they may be, whether at work, at home, or elsewhere.

Values are desirable, and we think they are worth pursuing, and we want to pursue them consistently, even when other desires compete with them. However, competing desires may capture our attention. For example, ordering a second dessert at a celebratory meal does not necessarily mean I no longer value my long-term health. In this particular instance, I may simply be making an exception to how I usually act on that commitment.

As guiding principles, values serve not only as the lens through which we perceive our experiences, but they also become strong factors in how we choose to act. For example, people who value autonomy over security may see their job as stifling and look for other opportunities; those who value security over autonomy see the same job as stable and dependable.

When I talk about values, I like to say that values are things that we value, things we care about. This simple sentence shifts our attention from abstract concepts to the things we hold close and see as part of who we are. It also lets us see the difference between ordering that second dessert and working to be trustworthy. The former satisfies a momentary desire; the latter speaks to an enduring concern.

Comparing what we say matters to us with how we consistently act can reveal a gap between our values and behavior. Imagine someone who says they value their personal relationships, but they repeatedly choose work over spending time with friends and family. This discrepancy between what a person says and what they do should bring reflection. It may be that the person does value personal relationships, but their competing value of financial security or personal ambition has a stronger influence on their decision-making. Alternatively, they may truly prioritize personal relationships but lose sight of values when responding to workplace demands. Sometimes, however, someone may recognize their priorities clearly and still have limited freedom to act because their job is insecure or their family depends on their income. Importantly, we can examine whether our repeated behaviors reflect what we value and consider what choices would help us act more consistently on what we care about.

Bas Verplanken and Rob Holland found that values influence people’s choices and behavior when they are brought into focus and when those values are central to the person’s self-concept.

To bring your values into your choices and actions, follow these four steps:

With regular practice, your values will become more than a list of admirable qualities; they will shape your goals, guide your decisions, and motivate you to act on what matters to you.

#4778. Acne Scars, Begone

These dermatologist-approved treatments can get your skin smooth again, reduce hyperpigmentation, and may even make you look a little younger.

Treating adult acne can feel like one big science experiment—until now. This is the guy’s guide to adult acne. Read the rest of the stories here.

ACNE SUCKS. THE scars it can leave behind suck even more. These dermatologist-approved* treatments can get your skin smooth again, reduce hyperpigmentation, and may even make you look a little younger.

These are known as atrophic scars and are caused when inflammation breaks down skin’s collagen that’s responsible for smoothness and elasticity. There are three main forms of atrophic scars, and some people will develop a mix of all of them.

Meet the icepick scar, so named because it looks as if your skin was pierced with something thin and pointed.

Derms will typically combine topical trichloroacetic acid (TCA) with a CO2 laser to supercharge the production of new collagen and resurface skin. Often, up to three sessions are needed and typically range in cost from $300 to $5,000 per session, depending on the size of the scar(s) and whether treatments are combined.

Commonly referred to as boxcar scars, this type of scar doesn’t run as deep as their icepick brethren and may respond to less invasive treatments.

The Treatment: Fraxel FTX or Microneedling

Your doctor may use a slightly more superficial fractionated laser (like the new nonablative Fraxel FTX). This procedure is around $1,000 per session. Another option is a microneedling treatment (tiny needles penetrate the skin to kick-start collagen), which can be paired with heat-like radiofrequency for better results. Multiple sessions at $600 to $1,500 a pop are typically necessary.

These rolling scars are slightly different, caused, yes, by collagen loss, but also when acne inflammation tethers areas of skin to the tissue below.

One option is a technique called subcision (which ranges anywhere from $300 to $1,500)—your doc will cut away the tethers pulling the skin downward to release the scar. Another option is Bellafill (roughly $800 per syringe), a type of filler that adds volume to depressed areas, or hyaluronic acid fillers (roughly $650 per syringe), which also lifts depressed areas to the same level as the surrounding skin.

You’re dealing with a hypertrophic scar or a keloid, which typically result from severe, deep cystic or nodular acne.

The hallmark signs of a standard hypertrophic scar, these signal that your body’s response to injury is to churn out way more collagen than you need. These scars are more common among people with darker skin tones.

Corticosteroid injections (roughly $100 to $300 per injection) flatten and soften excess scar tissue. A fractional CO2 laser breaks up the collagen, reduces the size of the scars, and helps injected or applied medications penetrate more effectively.

Think of this—called a keloid—as a hypertrophic scar on steroids. An apropos analogy, as that’s what you’ll use to treat it, too.

Corticosteroid injections will most likely be needed to break apart this large, fibrous collection of collagen tissue, but CO2 or fractionated lasers can be used afterward to improve the skin’s texture.

*Reviewed by Bradley Glodny, MD, and Rishi Chopra, MD.

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following a successful surgery, the Vatican said.

The Pope, 71, underwent surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic in Rome on October 13 to remove a nodule from his right lung. This was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

The surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s lung to “ensure a radical procedure; the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the Director of Vatican Healthcare Services, and Professor Stephano Margaritora, the lead surgeon, in a press release.

“An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations,” they said.

Pope Leo was in the operating room for 3 hours, while the operation itself lasted around 90 minutes.

The doctors noted that it was a successful operation with no complications.

According to Matteo Bruni, the Director of the Holy See Press Office, the Pope asked for dinner after the surgery and spent the evening with his secretaries and other Vatican staff.

In a press release on Wednesday, the Vatican said that the Pope’s postoperative recovery is progressing well.

According to Vatican News, Pope Leo had a calm first night following his surgery.

In the coming days, exams will be conducted on the removed tissue. There has currently been no change in the initially announced week of hospitalization.

On October 14, the Pope underwent blood tests and chest X-rays that were scheduled following his surgery. The results of these tests confirm that his postoperative recovery is progressing as expected, and the values are within a normal range for the type of operation performed.

Pope Leo has also undergone some respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room, the Vatican said.

It has not yet been announced whether he will require any further treatment.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer globally. It accounts for around 40% of all lung cancer diagnoses.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which accounts for about 80–85% of all lung cancers.

Lung adenocarcinoma begins in the epithelial cells that produce mucus. It is the most common type of NSCLC.

Adenocarcinoma can be classified further by the genetic changes driving the tumor. For example, EGFR-positive lung cancer is found more often in people who have never smoked and can often be treated with targeted therapies, which is why biomarker testing of tumor tissue helps guide treatment decisions.

Treatment for NSCLC is generally determined by the stage. However, it typically involves one or a combination of:

Surgery is generally the first step in treatment for this type of lung cancer. The right lung has three lobes, or sections, and the left has two.

A doctor will often remove the entire lobe that has the tumor in order to remove the tumor and improve the outlook.

The body eventually adapts in order to compensate for the loss of function.

According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), for NSCLC that hasn’t spread outside of the lung, the 5-year relative survival rate is 67%.
