#4736. Zero Motorcycles unveils $8K electric motorcycle, street-legal dirt bike, and much more

Zero Motorcycles is celebrating its 20th anniversary with a major wave of announcements at EICMA 2026, unveiling several new electric two-wheelers alongside some important technology upgrades that could make its existing motorcycles even more appealing.

The biggest news is an entirely new lightweight electric street motorcycle known as Project Ventura, designed to bridge the gap between the increasingly popular world of electric bikes plus lightweight e-motos and the full-size electric motorcycle market. But that’s far from the only news coming out of Zero’s booth in Milan.

The electric motorcycle maker is also announcing a new street-legal version of its XE electric dirt bike that was previously only street-legal in Europe, introducing its LS3 electric scooter to Europe, introducing a redesigned smartphone app, and sharing more details about its upcoming DC fast-charging system.

There’s quite a bit to unpack here, so let’s get into it.

Perhaps the most exciting announcement is Project Ventura, a new lightweight electric motorcycle that Zero hopes will attract an entirely new generation of riders.

With supermoto-inspired styling, 17-inch wheels, and a more approachable design than the company’s larger street motorcycles, Ventura appears aimed squarely at riders who want something more substantial than a typical lightweight e-moto but aren’t necessarily looking for a full-size, high-performance motorcycle.

And with a targeted price of less than US $8,000, it could be one of Zero’s most accessible street motorcycles yet.

The bike features a new electric powertrain producing over 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, delivering a sustained top speed of 65 mph (105 km/h) and a momentary maximum speed of 81 mph (130 km/h).

That’s a particularly interesting distinction, as it positions the bike as being able to briefly reach highway-capable speeds with the occasional burst of extra performance, but perhaps not for longer sustained highway stretches.

Importantly, we don’t yet know the battery capacity, though Zero is giving us a hint by publishing a range estimate. The company is quoting an estimated real-world range of 93 miles (150 km), but without a real battery capacity figure to parse, it’s hard to take that range estimate at face value.

We do know that the bike will feature onboard Level 2 charging, allowing riders to plug into public AC charging stations without carrying around a separate external charger – something more common on the smallest of electric motorcycles that attempt to cut down on weight and cost by using an off-board charger.

Other features include standard ABS, Bluetooth connectivity, integration with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app, and a chassis designed to accommodate a passenger.

The riding position is upright, and the bike’s supermoto-inspired geometry is intended to deliver agile handling and a playful riding experience.

Perhaps most interestingly, Zero isn’t hiding the fact that it sees the explosion of e-bikes and smaller electric motos as a potential gateway to motorcycle ownership.

“When we set out to build Project Ventura, we had three guiding principles: first, build a bike so good-looking you’d want its poster above your bed. Second, make it a proper electric motorcycle that feels like a natural next step for the millions of riders who’ve spent the last four or five years on e-bikes and e-motos. And third, make it ridiculously fun to ride,” explained Jim Callahan, Zero’s Chief Product and Partnerships Officer.

That’s a notable strategy for a company that has historically focused heavily on higher-performance electric motorcycles. However, the launch of Zero’s smaller Sur Ron-style electric dirt bikes last summer showed that the motorcycle maker did see the writing on the wall in terms of the success of the e-moto market compared to larger flagship bikes.

Instead of trying to convince existing gasoline motorcycle riders to make the electric switch, Zero is increasingly looking toward younger riders who may have already fallen in love with electric two-wheelers and are ready for something faster and more capable.

But for those interested in the new Ventura, they’ll have to wait just a bit longer. The motorcycle is expected to become available in summer 2027.

Another major announcement is a new street-legal version of Zero’s XE electric dirt bike.

The original XE was introduced as part of Zero’s more affordable X Line of lightweight electric off-road motorcycles, offering a more accessible entry point to the brand than its traditional street and dual-sport models. While the model was available in street-legal format in Europe, the US versions were purely off-road affairs.

Now Zero is taking that same general concept and making it legal for public roads, opening up significantly more riding possibilities.

The new XE is fully homologated and features the necessary street equipment, including a headlight, taillight, and centrally mounted dashboard. A small integrated flyscreen and black bodywork give the motorcycle a more refined appearance, while wide dual-sport tires help it transition between pavement and dirt.

Zero has also revised the gearing, using a rear sprocket designed to balance off-road performance with the higher speeds required for street riding.

The result is a claimed top speed of 60 mph (97 km/h), making the XE capable of considerably more than simply putting around the neighborhood, though with a slight torque sacrifice.

For riders who live near off-road riding areas, the appeal is obvious. Instead of loading a dirt bike into a truck or trailer to reach the trails, owners could potentially ride directly from home to the trailhead, provided local regulations allow it.

That’s a particularly useful capability for a lightweight electric dirt bike, where much of the appeal comes from its simplicity, low maintenance, and ability to explore places that larger motorcycles might struggle to reach.

The new street-legal XE is expected to launch in spring 2027, with pricing starting at US $6,295.

Zero is also expanding its electric scooter offerings with the European debut of the LS3, a faster and more capable scooter designed for urban transportation and longer commutes.

While Zero has traditionally been associated with electric motorcycles, its growing interest in scooters represents another effort to reach riders who prioritize everyday transportation over outright performance.

The LS3 offers a top speed of 75 mph (121 km/h), which puts it well beyond the typical low-speed urban electric scooter category.

Zero also quotes a range of up to 93 miles (150 km), powered by a battery system consisting of three onboard batteries with a combined capacity of 5.6 kWh.

Interestingly, one of those batteries is removable and located beneath the seat. Riders can remove it to free up additional storage space, offering some flexibility between maximum battery capacity and cargo-carrying convenience.

That could prove useful for commuters who don’t always need the scooter’s full range but would appreciate extra room for everyday items.

The LS3 also comes equipped with heated grips and a heated seat, features that should be particularly welcome to European riders commuting through colder months.

Connected technology rounds out the package, including compatibility with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app.

The LS3 is expected to become available in Europe in spring 2027.

Beyond the new vehicles, Zero is also working on a redesigned smartphone application that promises to give riders considerably more control over their motorcycles.

The new app is being developed for the LS3, 2027 Street and Dual Sport motorcycles, and Project Ventura.

One of the more interesting features is the ability to customize riding modes. In addition to preset modes that adjust power delivery and regenerative braking, riders will be able to create a custom mode and individually tune parameters including speed, power, torque, and regeneration.

The app will also include a charging-station finder, allowing riders to search for nearby chargers and filter them by charging speed, network, and availability. Apple Maps integration will provide route guidance to selected charging locations.

An optional ride-history feature can automatically record trips, including their distance, duration, and route previews.

Riders will also be able to customize their motorcycle’s dashboard layout, choosing which information appears in each quadrant of the display.

Battery management is getting some attention, too. The app will provide controls for scheduled charging, target charge levels, charging limits, and long-term battery storage settings.

Zero is also adding integrated feedback and support tools that allow owners to report problems or suggest improvements directly through the app, including photos and diagnostic logs.

The redesigned app is expected to arrive in 2027.

Perhaps the most consequential technology announcement, at least for riders who want to take their electric motorcycles beyond short commutes and weekend rides, is Zero’s continued development of DC fast charging.

Zero says it is targeting a 2027 launch for its new fast-charging system, which will support compatible Street and Dual Sport motorcycles.

The system is being designed to charge compatible batteries from 20% to 80% in less than 30 minutes.

That’s a major improvement in convenience compared to the longer AC charging stops that have traditionally been associated with Zero motorcycles.

Importantly, the company is developing the system for both North America and Europe, with different charging connectors for each market.

European motorcycles will use the CCS standard, while North American models will feature NACS connectors.

The latter is particularly interesting given the growing adoption of NACS charging infrastructure across North America, potentially making it easier for electric motorcycle riders to access a wider range of charging locations.

Zero is also developing a retrofit option for eligible existing motorcycles, meaning some current owners may eventually be able to upgrade their bikes rather than purchasing entirely new models to take advantage of the technology.

The company hasn’t yet announced pricing or a complete list of compatible motorcycles, and the retrofit option remains under development.

Still, the prospect of adding significantly faster charging to existing electric motorcycles could be an important development for the brand.

There are several exciting announcements here, but I think the biggest takeaway is that Zero seems to be increasingly focused on making electric motorcycling more accessible through smaller and more affordable options.

For much of its 20-year history, Zero has been a pioneer in the electric motorcycle industry, often offering impressive performance and technology, but at prices that made its motorcycles difficult for many riders to justify. The bikes have long won acclaim, but $20k was a big ask.

The company’s more affordable X Line bikes have already demonstrated that Zero is interested in attracting riders who might never have considered one of its larger electric motorcycles. The street-legal XE takes that concept a step further, and Project Ventura could be an even more important addition.

I’m particularly intrigued by Zero’s explicit acknowledgment that millions of people have spent the last several years riding e-bikes and smaller electric motos, and that many of those riders may be ready to graduate to something bigger.

That’s an audience I’ve been watching grow for years. These are riders who are already comfortable with electric drivetrains, who appreciate the simplicity of twist-and-go riding, and who don’t necessarily have any attachment to gasoline engines or traditional motorcycle culture.

For those riders, a lightweight, fun electric motorcycle capable of 81 mph and priced below $8,000 could be an awfully compelling next step.

The new street-legal XE is similarly exciting, especially for riders who want to combine urban transportation with off-road adventures without needing a truck to haul their bike around.

During the late 60’s to the early 70’s the in thing in motorcycles was the street legal dirt bike. I had a 1971 model Kawasaki 125 street legal dirtbike that I bought for $525 and it was great for getting around as a kid. When this street legal type of EV bike goes below $5000 it could be the next big thing.

And while the new motorcycles are likely to get most of the attention, I wouldn’t overlook the DC fast-charging announcement. Charging speed has long been one of the biggest limitations facing electric motorcycles, particularly for riders interested in longer trips. A sub-30-minute charging stop isn’t quite gasoline-level convenience, but it’s getting much closer to something that can work for real motorcycle touring.

Of course, several important details remain unknown, and we’ll have to wait until 2027 to see how these products and technologies perform in the real world.

But taken together, these announcements suggest Zero is making a serious effort to expand beyond its traditional audience and build electric motorcycles for a much broader range of riders.

And after two decades of helping pioneer the electric motorcycle industry, that’s exactly the kind of evolution I’d like to see.

The blades are about as spaced out from each other as I’ve seen on any razor, which helps prevent clogging—something that is even more common when dealing with thick body hair.

Surrounding the two blades are a lubricating strip, an anti-ingrown bar, and an anti-irritation bar that work to reduce friction and help prevent trapped hairs. Plus, the blade head sits on a flexible pivoting disc, which helps the razor follow the contours of your body for smoother, more consistent contact with the skin.

Testing Notes: I’m not usually one to go completely bald below the waist, but this razor makes a strong case for it. It left my skin smooth and irritation-free without any lingering bumps in the days following, which is something I’ve found to be common when dealing with body razors. The grip is incredible and the pivoting head makes getting into the nooks and crannies of your body easy.

Before diving into the most intimate of manscaping, it’s important to consider a few key components of the device you’ll be using, given the sensitivity of the region. Not only to avoid any dreaded nicks or cuts, but also to ensure that the process is completed as seamlessly as possible.

Whenever you’re dealing with a trimmer of any kind, the battery life is one of the most prominent considerations. No one wants their device to sputter out and die when they’ve only managed to trim half their beard, and the same is true for the nether regions. Sure, it may be less noticeable than having half a beard, but it can still be uncomfortable. Look for devices that can hold a charge for at least an hour; this should guarantee you two to three sessions per charge.

Any less and you’re going to have to really be diligent with charging after every use or run the risk of it dying out before the next job’s done. The easiest way to avoid this scenario is to look for a rechargeable device, but more on that in a sec.

If you’re a committed pubic trimmer and never travel without one, look for the lighter options to ensure you can comfortably keep them in a carry-on or bag without weighing yourself down. While the TSA and airlines do not generally have a weight limit specifically for grooming devices, they do limit the weight of your bags, so we recommend sticking to trimmers that are under 10 oz to avoid too much bulk. Plus, if you’re new to this type of thing, steering away from tools that are heavier than this until you get a better idea of the process will help you avoid any painful slip-ups.

Similarly, how often do you change up your overall manscaping look? If you find yourself often changing up lengths and styles, you’re going to want to grab a device with multiple attachments and length options. The Braun Series 9 is the best-case scenario here, as it comes packed with nine attachments that create a total of 40 (!) length options. On the other hand, if you typically go full bald or keep it one consistent length, focus on the device’s head shape and blade material or close shaving ability rather than the number of attachments.

For the closest shave (outside of a cartridge razor), look to stainless steel or metal blades, as these can handle the most motor power and are more adept at plowing through thicker hair. While most of the trimmers on this list (and pubic trimmers in general) do not list their official motor power, having stainless steel blades is often the best indicator of a powerful tool, as it shows the brand looks towards the highest quality materials and performance available.

Not to mention, stainless steel blades are typically easier to clean. That being said, the risk of nicks and cuts is higher, so if you’re new to pubic trimming, opt for ceramic or plastic blades. These are gentler on skin, though they won’t get you as close to bare skin.

Use a rechargeable pubic trimmer to avoid mid-trim shutdowns and eliminate the need for spare batteries. Keep it charged between 30 percent and 80 percent to maintain performance and prevent it from dying when you need it most.

Do you prefer to do your manscaping in or outside of the shower? There is no wrong answer, but whichever you prefer is worth keeping in mind when choosing a trimmer. Some are made to be used wet, like the Philips Norelco OneBlade, while others not so much. If you’re a dedicated shower groomer, focus on the fully waterproof options.

As Men’s Health’s grooming editor, I test electric razors and similar devices for a living. When it comes to pubic trimmers, we’ve been testing these devices for nearly three years since this story was first published in 2023. For this update, I tested or retested over 15 pubic trimmers and razors, while consulting with skin and haircare experts on which tools they recommend in 2026.

I also considered top-reviewed trimmers that had high customer ratings on trusted e-commerce websites. After putting each device to the test, I evaluated its effectiveness, safety, and value. Following 12 months of testing, these seven tools proved to be the best for the job.

1. First and foremost, make sure you have ample time and are not rushed. This is not something you want to speed through.

2. Position yourself in front of a mirror with good lighting to make sure you have good visibility for all the crevices.

3. Grab your trimmer and pick your desired length. If you plan to fully shave your pubic hair, set the length long enough to shave easily but not too long—about a couple of days’ worth of stubble. If you’re trimming, start with a longer setting than you want at first; you can always trim it shorter later.

4. Apply baby powder on your pubic area while it’s dry to help soak up extra moisture and plump up the hair.

5. With short, gentle strokes, use the trimmer to cut the hair. Pubic hair grows in a variety of directions, so you’ll want to go slow and possibly go over the same areas a few times. For your scrotum and shaft, go extra slow and stretch the skin to flatten it and make it easier to trim. If you’re trimming your buttcheeks, crack, or perineum, you may want to place a hand mirror on the floor to help see where you’re trimming. You can also place one leg on a tub or toilet to make the area easier to see.

6. If you’re happy with the trim job, then you’re done! Hop in the shower to wash off.

7. If you’re going to shave completely, once you’re out of the shower, apply a pre-shave oil and shaving cream to the areas you’re going to shave. The key here is not to be stingy with the cream.

8. When you’re taking a razor to your nether regions, you’ll want to be extra careful. Shave with the grain of the hair in short, slow strokes. Do not—I repeat—do not rush. You’ll want to use the same stretching technique on your scrotum and shaft as you did while trimming, and the mirror is ideal if you’re taking the razor around back.

9. Make sure to rinse the razor frequently to avoid clogs and reapply shaving cream as needed.

10. Once you’re done, hop back in the shower to rinse everything away.

11. Apply a moisturizer or body oil to the area to help keep it protected. You may also want to apply a moisturizer or anti-chafe product regularly (like at least once a day) to help reduce friction, which can cause irritation on shaved skin, especially below the belt.

Maybe you’re a regular manscaper, or perhaps you just took the plunge into trimming out your nether regions. Regardless, one truth holds true: As soon as you take off the hair, it blooms right back again.

Sure, it might seem that your pubic hair is on a steroid-fueled regrowth. But that’s actually something of an optic illusion, says Dr. Alexes Hazen, MD, a reconstructive and cosmetic plastic surgeon at NYU Langone Health.

People who trim or shave their pubic hair often believe it grows faster than the hair on their head, but that’s a misconception, she says. We merely notice hair growth more and its speed when it’s shorter.

With pubic hair—and other body hair—the entire process takes about 30 to 44 days, Dr. Hazen says. That means the same pubes that started to grow will shed in about a month to a month and a half.

#4734. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4733. BYD’s 3,000-hp EV crashes at about 280 mph — Watch the driver escape unharmed

BYD’s electric supercar delivers an insane nearly 3,000 hp from four electric motors. During a high-speed test, the Yangwang U9 Extreme crashed at about 280 mph, but the driver walked away unharmed.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme is a “dream car,” as BYD calls it, a souped-up, track-focused version of its electric hypercar.

After it became the world’s fastest production car last year, reaching a top speed of 496.22 km/h, or about 308 mph, BYD is attempting to beat it by breaking the 500 km/h (310 mph) mark.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme features the world’s first mass-produced 1,200V ultra-high-voltage platform and BYD’s e4 platform.

The quad-motor setup is the first in the world rated at 30,000 rpm, BYD said, delivering nearly 3,000 hp (3,000 PS) combined.

While BYD is preparing to attempt a run this month, the company shared a video of the Yangwang U9 Xtreme crashing in a violent high-speed test.

During the first run, it clocked over 350 km/h (217 mph), no problem. On the second run, it hit over 420 km/h (261 mph).

However, during the third run, BYD was attempting to reach over 450 km/h (280 mph) when the vehicle violently crashed into the guardrail and continued spinning out of control. You can see some of the footage from inside the vehicle.

BYD said that after a comprehensive medical exam, the hospital found the driver in good health with no serious injuries.

When I was still in law enforcement, we did some pursuit driving training and you learn a lot about the dynamics of a vehicle. It's amazing just how quickly and badly something can go wrong at just 100 mph let alone nearly triple that speed. The fact is that the average person can't drive to the max limits of a basic car like a Corolla let alone super cars.

Is it time to reign in the HP and speed wars? Do we need vehicles that can do 0-60 in less than 3 seconds? Unless these companies begin to require 40+ hour specialized training courses in order to buy/operate these high HP vehicles today, then maybe it's time to stop the silly push for more.

And BTW. No matter what the performance levels are of any cars today, I still feel that it would be smart to push legal driving age to at least 17 or 18 instead of 16 and make getting a DL harder to do with way more emphasis on driver's education training.

The vehicle’s high-strength carbon-fiber cabin also held up impressively despite the front and rear damage.

It didn’t take long for BYD to try again, reaching a top speed of 457.89 km/h (284.5 mph) on the next run. Jiang Gong, one of Yangwang’s riders, said he sees some leeway and believes it can break 500 km/h (310 mph).

At the end of the video, BYD said (translated into English), “The ultimate pursuit has no end; the summit will eventually be reached.”

#4732. Don't Let Conflict Erode Your Relationship

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Couples can argue over even the slightest difference of opinion. It can be as simple as preferring different kinds of breakfast cereals. You want the healthy organic variety, and your partner wants the sugar-coated flakes he had as a child. This trivial dispute often escalates until, in the worst-case scenario, you’re ready to break up.

How did things get so out of control? If you love someone, you should be able to handle some daily bickering. Relationship researchers often point out ways that conflicts become dysfunctional. In the newest approach, focus is placed on emotional regulation as the key to neutralizing some of these unpleasant interactions.

In a new approach to understanding relationship difficulties, University of Quebec’s Aurélie Thuot-Jolicoeur and colleagues (2026) posed a conflict-ridden scenario at the outset of their paper. A couple argues over how to spend some of their time while on a Parisian vacation. But instead of luxuriating in the lovely scenery and enjoying all that Paris has to offer, they began to quibble over whether to see a museum on one of their precious days in the French capital. One partner excitedly suggested this activity, but the other shot her down, claiming to be too tired. Suspecting this was an excuse for disinterest, the protagonist in this story becomes distressed. Over the next few days, the memory popped up unexpectedly, creating renewed emotional wounds.

In posing the alternative to this unpleasant outcome, the authors suggest that the distressed partner could acknowledge feeling upset and then ask why the partner wasn’t interested. Empathizing with the partner rather than becoming upset could enhance the relationship as they “form a more understanding and insightful attitude”

If you’ve ever been in a situation such as this (maybe not in Paris…), you can undoubtedly feel some empathy for each relationship partner as the original scenario unfolded. To get from scenario one to scenario two, the authors suggest, requires that you engage your emotion regulation strategies. To do so, they propose, involves the motivational approach known as Self-Determination Theory (SDT). According to SDT, instead of avoiding conflict or reacting immaturely by sulking or yelling, you are better off using integrative regulation, in which you allow yourself to notice and ultimately accept your emotions, even the unpleasant ones. You can now enter into a conflict constructively as you seek to learn from the conflict about your own emotions and those of your partner.

Based on SDT, the U. Quebec authors proposed that it’s not conflict alone that causes problems; it’s also the tendency to ruminate unproductively over a past disagreement with your partner. The memory of an event, they suggest, can be just as important as the event itself, especially if it fails to be resolved or brings up unpleasant emotions. You need to be able to control your emotions when those memories pop up in much the same way you do when encountering the situation in the first place.

To test this idea, Thuot-Jolicoeur et al. asked participants to describe a memory of a significant conflict they experienced with a partner. To measure emotion regulation from the SDT perspective, they asked participants to rate items tapping dysregulation (“When I feel negative emotions, I can’t concentrate on the other things I have to do”) and integrative regulation (“On occasions, feeling negative emotions helped me to understand something about the situation I was in”). These were part of the dispositional emotion regulation questions. Separately, the authors rated the extent to which these strategies were used in the recalled event itself.

The conflicts couples brought into the study included these three themes: (1) sexuality and intimacy; (2) needs, values, and interpersonal differences; and (3) practical conflicts. Relationship quality was the outcome of the analyses using emotion regulation of each partner as predictors.

As hypothesized, when partners used integrative regulation when recalling a conflict, their relationship satisfaction was higher than when they used dysfunctional regulation. Over time, the authors proposed, if the recall of a conflicted memory prompts renewed use of dysregulated strategies (hostility, withdrawal, or rumination), the negative effects will only increase exponentially, driving the couple members further apart. If, instead, couples put the conflict in the rearview mirror through integrative regulation, they can move toward greater closeness and understanding.

Knowing that the dysregulated recall of a troubling event with your partner can be as detrimental to your relationship as the event itself can be helpful as you and your partner try to move past the difficult emotions. As in the Parisian vacation example, the partner who felt hurt and dismissed could use these feelings to gain important self-insights. Maybe the partner truly was tired and needed time to rest and refresh. This doesn’t mean that the partner had somehow fallen out of love or was otherwise ready to move on from the relationship.

Reworking the recall of an event that caused distress can help to nip your feelings of being hurt and rejected in the bud. Furthermore, as you try to move on, it can also be helpful to isolate the event itself as the cause of your distress rather than generalize to everything being wrong in the entire relationship. Sharing your feelings in a nonthreatening or non-accusatory way can get you and your partner onto a path toward greater understanding.

To sum up, relationships are never 100 percent smooth going, but zeroing in on the conflicts—and their memory—that shape your relationship can help you move from dysfunction to emotional acceptance.

Thuot-Jolicoeur, A., Mérette, V. S., Lapointe, V. A., Carbonneau, N., & Philippe, F. L. (2026). Emotion regulation in couples’ conflict memories: A dyadic examination of relationship quality. Journal of Family Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/fam0001555

We're talking a fabric so luxurious that it makes regular cotton feel rough in comparison. Based on our testing, this pair of trunks nails the perfect balance of stretch and structure with their four-way stretch, so they move with you no matter how active (or lazy) your day gets.

Unlike other trunks that call for constant tugging or readjusting, these stayed perfectly in place, whether we were sitting, standing, or running errands around town. The quick-draw fly makes using the bathroom easier and faster in the middle of the night. On humid days, these are a lifesaver. Despite us breaking a sweat, this underwear stayed fresh, which speaks to their exceptional level of odor resistance. And even after multiple washes, the softness doesn't diminish—a true sign of premium quality.

Sunspel’s Classic Boxer Shorts are hands down some of the best out there, and once you try them, you’ll get it. This pair is made by a U.K. brand with over a century of experience perfecting the essentials, so it's time-tested. These boxers are cut from long-staple cotton, meaning the fibers are longer, the fabric is softer, and it'll last for the long haul. Basically, it feels ridiculously comfortable—like you’re lounging in luxury every time you put it on—and it stays that way wear after wear.

One standout feature is the distinctive back panel. Sunspel uses a single smooth panel across the rear versus an uncomfortable central seam running down the middle. For us, that meant no chafing, no awkward pressure, and no irritation, even when we were sitting at our work desk or running quick errands. The fabric is lightweight but strong, so it breathes well and never bunches under pants. During testing, it held up all day, no matter what: long commutes, walking tours on vacation, or casual bike rides. We don't recommend wearing this pair under gym shorts, but you can reserve it for days of less sweat-inducing activity since it's all cotton.

They’ve got this easy, relaxed fit that gives you full range of motion, but the tailoring keeps them from feeling baggy or sloppy. And then there’s the design: They’re finished with a super gentle waistband that sits comfortably. We also love that there's solid colors as well as striped patterns. It's the kind that makes you rethink the whole category. They’re built for comfort but stylish enough to feel special, which is exactly what you want from a pair you’ll wear day in and day out.

I normally wouldn’t trust underwear that costs under $10 to compete with premium pairs, but Uniqlo’s trunks are the exception. The Japanese retailer offers some of the best basics around, delivering impressive quality at an affordable price, including these boxer shorts, which are especially comfortable in the heat. They’re made with a breathable woven cotton fabric, which feels much lighter than any knit underwear I own. When the temps went up to 100 degrees in New York last week, these kept me cool all day.

The fit is more open and roomy than my briefs, so my crown jewels had plenty of breathing room and even caught a breeze when I was lounging around. I also love how they lie flat under shorts and linen pants, though I would skip wearing slim trousers since the fabric can bunch. Even though the waistband is scrunched, it sits gently against my skin without causing any irritation. When my Sunspel pair is in the laundry, I’ll even wear it to bed on warm nights. For such an inexpensive style, it holds up over time. I’ve washed it multiple times without seeing a single loose seam or noticing any shrinkage. Plus, the striped pattern looks timeless, so it doesn’t feel like a bargain-bin underwear.

I can always count on mesh fabric to keep me cool when I need it most, which is why I love this underwear. SAXX uses a polyester-elastane mesh with an open, dotted texture that lets heat and moisture escape, so I never feel clammy. Even when I sweat, the fabric never gets waterlogged and dries incredibly fast. It’s one of my go-to pairs for workouts, especially on heavy cardio days. The hammock-style pouch keeps everything secure and supported while I’m biking or running on the treadmill, and the fit is snugger than most boxer shorts, specifically around the butt, thigh, and legs.

The 6-inch inseam stops mid-thigh, while the high waist sits right under your belly button. I can wear them under just about any pair of pants without worrying about bunching or visible lines. The compression-like fit may feel too snug if you prefer a roomier boxer short. And the mesh fabric isn’t as soft or natural-feeling as cotton or modal, so it may not be everyone’s favorite pair for lounging all day. The good thing is the pack of three can get you through half the week, especially if you stock up.

If you’re ready to upgrade from basic cotton underwear, CDLP is where I’d start. I love the Tencel Lyocell fabric that has an incredibly silky, almost cooling feel against my skin. It’s surprisingly breathable, too, so I never feel overheated on days when the temps spike to 90 degrees. It strikes a nice balance between feeling luxurious and being practical. The snug fit hugs my body without squeezing too tightly. It rests just below the waist and has a 3.8-inch inseam that sits high on the upper thigh and hides under my short shorts. Some of the more expensive pairs tend to pill, but the fabric on this one keeps its smooth, premium feel even after multiple washes. The only real drawback is the price, but if you’re willing to splurge on a single pair of underwear, the comfort makes it feel well worth it.

Quality underwear doesn't have to cost a fortune. Take Uniqlo's Airism Ultra Seamless Boxer Briefs, which clock in under $20 and also fit like a glove. During my testing, the cutoff waist felt invisible, sitting flush against the skin without squeezing or rolling, like it was made just for me. Despite its close-hugging cut, there's a fair amount of stretch to accommodate you running up the stairs, twisting in your chair, or walking briskly through crowded city streets.

Overall, I found this pair to be lightweight, super breathable, and packed with new moisture-wicking technology that helps to keep you fresh, cool, and dry around the clock. Whether it's a hot day or you're working up a sweat at the gym, Airism pulls moisture away from your skin, making sure you don't feel swampy down under.

Every Sunday at my house is wash day, but this underwear has survived through every last cycle without losing its allure. Our only gripe is that Uniqlo Airism sells out very fast, which means you have to wait for the occasional restock—so get them now.

Cotton is the OG of underwear fabrics, and our testers found that it's the most comfortable knit for everyday fits. Take note: while cotton is pretty breathable, it doesn't do a great job of wicking away moisture. That's why our fashion editors do not recommend cotton skivvies for working out. In some cases, a pair of undies that's 100% cotton tends to lose shape over time and can give a swamp-ass feeling. If you have money to spend, we recommend trying a long-staple or organic cotton, which is more premium and durable.

Nylon is moisture-wicking and super durable, so the fabric won’t pill or stretch out. However, a little spandex (aka elastane) in the fabric helps for movement and extra comfort. Plus, it dries quickly too, so you won't feel sticky post-workout.

Imagine cotton, but smoother and a little fancier. Modal has a silky-soft feel that's light and cool against your skin. Testers say their favorite modal boxer briefs almost disappear under their clothes.

If you're looking to keep your precious cargo secure, then briefs provide the most security. However, if you want to let the package breathe, then boxers are your best bet. Remember: Boxers tend to ride up when you're wearing slim pants, which is why we recommend only wearing them with more relaxed fits.

If you need extra support, we recommend underwear with a pouch or a snugger fit around the waistband. For some men with testicular pain or discomfort, they may want to find a style that fits well and doesn't ride up or bunch, as this could aggravate their symptoms.

Your underwear is the first thing you put on and the last thing you take off, so it has to work with you, not against you, all day long. If it doesn't do its job, you'll feel it, whether it's discomfort, chafing, or overheating.

Think about it: excellent underwear isn't just about looking cool (though that's like icing on the cake). It's about how it performs in real life. Are you lounging at home? Going for a long run? Stuck on a flight for hours? Each of these scenarios demands something different. You need underwear that supports your lifestyle, whether that's stretch for flexibility, moisture-wicking for sweat, or breathability to keep things fresh down yonder.

The best breathable underwear manages heat and moisture so sweat can escape instead of getting trapped against your skin. Many use micro-knit or mesh-like weaves that create tiny air channels within the fabric, allowing heat to dissipate and air to circulate as you move. Others incorporate moisture-wicking fibers to pull sweat away from the body and spread it across the surface of the fabric so it evaporates faster. Some brands even add targeted “cool zones” or thinner panels in high-sweat areas to boost airflow where you need it most.

When underwear can’t breathe, moisture builds up, leading to overheating, chafing, irritation, and odor. Breathable underwear works with your body by keeping things cooler, drier, and more comfortable throughout the day. For Men’s Health guys, breathability makes a difference for everyday wear, long commutes, desk jobs, workouts, travel days, and humid conditions. It’s especially clutch for guys who sweat easily, live in hot climates, train hard, or spend long stretches in the same pair from morning to night.

As part of the Men’s Health style team, led by our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, I’ve tested some of the best—and worst—underwear on the market firsthand. Since 2015, our team has worn, washed, and stressed-tested more than 100 pairs across every major style, brand, and fabric imaginable, from classic cotton briefs to high-tech performance boxer briefs and luxe everyday upgrades.

Testing wasn't limited to just one body type or fit preference. In addition to my own wear tests, multiple Men's Health editors with different builds pitched in, spanning sizes from small through XXL. This allowed us to see how each pair fit and performed across a wide range of body types, rises, thigh sizes, and proportions—and to flag issues like inconsistent sizing, rolling waistbands, or fabric that only works on one kind of frame.

I wore each pair repeatedly in real-life situations, including workdays, workouts, commutes, travel, and weekend outings. I looked at how each pair performed over time, paying close attention to whether fabrics remained soft without pilling, waistbands held their shape, seams avoided chafing, and support held up after hours of movement. I judged each pair on fabric quality, fit, breathability, odor control, stretch and recovery, durability after repeated washes, and comfort levels ranging from morning to night. Only the pairs that consistently delivered comfort, support, and long-term performance earned a spot on this list. What you’ll find here are the top 12 best men’s underwear options that rose to the top after years of hands-on testing by the Men’s Health team.

Boxers: They’re classic, loose-fitting shorts that are lightweight, with lots of breathing room, and zero restriction. They’re great for lounging or sleeping because they feel airy and relaxed, but that same looseness makes them less practical under slim pants. Fabric can bunch, ride up, and offer little to no support if you’re moving around a lot. Boxer briefs: They’re cut like boxers but fit snugly like briefs. That means they hug your thighs, hold everything in place, and layer smoothly under jeans, trousers, or even gym shorts. They also prevent chafing since the fabric creates a barrier between your thighs—a lifesaver if you walk a lot or hit the gym. The tradeoff? They’re less airy than boxers, but most guys prefer the balance of comfort, coverage, and support.

That really depends on your laundry schedule. If you’re someone who does laundry once a week, aim for at least 10 to 12 pairs so you’ve got a little cushion. If laundry happens less often—say every two weeks—you’ll probably want 15 to 20 pairs. If you’re very active, then consider stocking your drawer with 25 to 30 pairs. Basically, you want enough to last until wash day plus a couple extra for workouts, surprise trips, or the occasional lazy Sunday when you just don’t feel like doing laundry.

A good rule of thumb: it’s reasonable to refresh your stash every six to 12 months, but quality underwear can last longer depending on fabric, frequency of wear, washing, and condition. If the elastic’s shot, they’re sagging, developing holes, or the fabric’s thinning, that’s your cue to toss them. Think of it as a rotation—you don’t need to replace everything at once, but gradually swap in new pairs so you’re always stocked with comfortable, supportive ones.

Every man has worn them at some point; boxers are light and loose and so freeing. They're the classic underwear style for men that feels very relaxed with short legs. This type of underwear is perfect for lounging around the house, sleeping, or wearing under relaxed-fit pants. Also comes in a variety of prints and patterns (hello, personality).

Think speedo. Think upside-down triangle. Briefs provide the required coverage and optimal support while exposing more skin for ease of mobility. Here, there's no risk of leg fabric riding up (because there's none).

Perhaps the most popular one, it's a hybrid of loose-fit boxers and tight briefs, offering a solid balance of support and comfort. If you’re not a fan of underwear that rides up too high, go for boxer briefs that have a longer leg and a snug fit, like compression underwear that’s perfect for the gym. They should skim the leg versus squeezing you too tight.

Like the title says, a trunk is similar to boxer briefs but with a shorter cut—halfway up the thigh. It's best for guys who want something fitted but less fabric around the leg. For some visual assistance, think of trunks as the underwear style that most CK models wear on big billboards.

It depends on personal preference, comfort, and the activity. Here's a quick breakdown to help guide your choice, weighing the pros and cons of both.

Tight underwear (e.g., briefs, boxer briefs) provides better support, which is especially useful for physical activities like running or working out. This type reduces chafing and prevents excessive movement, which can help with comfort throughout the day. Works well under slim-fit pants, as it avoids bunching and creates a cleaner silhouette. If it's too tight, it can restrict airflow and potentially cause discomfort or sweating, especially in warmer weather. Overly tight fits might not be ideal for guys concerned about reproductive health, though the effect is typically negligible with properly sized underwear.

On the other hand, loose underwear is better suited for lounging or casual, low-impact activities since it allows more airflow and freedom of movement. It feels more breathable, making it ideal for hotter climates or relaxed settings. Also, loose underwear can be paired with loose-fit pants for added comfort. This option lacks support, which feel uncomfortable during workouts or physical activity. Plus, it can cramp your style—bunching up under tighter pants and offering a restrictive feel.

If you want to protect the structural integrity of your underwear's waistband, the best way to keep them from stretching is to hand wash them and hang them dry. But given how impractical that is, the second best option is to put them in the washing machine on cold water and use a low dryer setting so the elastic doesn't warp. However, our testers say that most of the pairs they've tried have kept their waistbands' shapes even after several trips to the laundromat. If your underwear's waistband has lost its shape, you're probably overdue to replace it.

Even the best underwear won’t last if you don’t take care of it properly. Washing underwear inside out helps remove sweat and bacteria more effectively while protecting the fabric’s surface. Cold or warm water is usually best, as hot water can break down elastic fibers and cause shrinkage over time. Skip harsh detergents and fabric softeners, especially for performance or moisture-wicking underwear. Softeners can coat fibers and reduce breathability and odor control. When possible, air-drying is ideal, as high heat from dryers is the fastest way to kill stretch and warp waistbands. If you do use a dryer, stick to low heat.

#4729. Tesla cuts FSD’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe

Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.

The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

The RDW’s notice is the clearest official confirmation of how the system was configured when the Dutch regulator approved FSD Supervised on April 10. The “speed margin,” which lets the system deviate from the detected limit for “safety and traffic flow,” could go up to +50%. On a 100 km/h highway, that’s 150 km/h. In a 30 km/h city zone, it’s 45 km/h.

Now the margin tops out at +10%. It also resets to 0% every time the car starts, and the RDW says other speed-related functions are now disabled by default. It didn’t say which ones.

The new name shows up on the in-car display, in the owner’s manual, and in other driver information on HW4 vehicles. Tesla pushes all of it over the air.

The RDW describes the update as “several minor changes” that Tesla asked it to assess. The regulator says it checked the implementation, found no adverse or unintended effects, and folded the changes into the existing type approval without amending or extending it. It also stresses that the rename doesn’t change what the system does. It’s still driver assistance, and the driver is still responsible.

The RDW notified the nine member states that recognize its approval: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. That’s 10 countries counting the Netherlands, up from eight at the start of October.

The EU-wide decision still sits with the Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV). The RDW says those talks are confidential and won’t comment on them. As we reported, the EU pushed the vote to December at the earliest, and passing it takes a qualified majority: 15 of 27 member states representing at least 65% of the EU population.

Speed has been the biggest problem for Tesla’s file in Brussels. In June, Sweden asked the EU to reject FSD unless Tesla removed the ability to set speeds above the posted limit. In September, a Brussels pedestrian safety group found the system speeding in 55% of the 30 km/h segments it tested, in a country that had already approved it. France has cited urban speeding as one of its reasons for refusing to recognize the Dutch approval.

Then, on October 6, Germany’s Transport Ministry said it would back EU approval after Tesla agreed to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name, which the ministry called misleading, and to cap speed tolerance at 10%. Today’s RDW update delivers both.

But 10% isn’t what Sweden asked for. Sweden wanted no setting above the limit at all. Several European countries are known for enforcing speed limits strictly.

Good, but that’s only part of the problem. Tesla’s biggest issue with FSD right now is that it doesn’t properly detect the speed limits.

Doing 10% over the limit in North America is almost expected. However, in Europe you can get a speeding ticket for 5 kms over the limit by an automated camera/radar system. When I rent a car over there I drive the posted limit.

Being locked at 10% over the limit doesn’t mean much if you don’t know the actual limit.

The name change is needed globally and it is past due. “Tesla Assisted Driving” describes what the system does. Meanwhile, Tesla still sells the exact same kind of software in the US as “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” for $99 a month. If it’s misleading in Berlin, it’s misleading in California.

Practically, this update gets Tesla Germany’s vote. The question for December is whether a 10% cap is enough for France, Italy, and Spain, or whether Sweden’s zero-tolerance line wins out.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Inside the shoes and layers the endurance athlete relies on for steep climbs.

RÉMI BONNET MAKES running up mountains look easy. The Swiss endurance athlete holds the world record for the vertical kilometer, having climbed more than 3,200 feet in just 27 minutes and 21 seconds. It’s the equivalent of running nearly three Empire State Buildings straight up in less than half an hour.

That's why Tudor, Rolex's adventurous younger brother and one of our favorite watch brands, tapped the 31-year-old athlete for its “Born to Dare” campaign, which celebrates high-achieving risk-takers. For Bonnet, that partnership means "daring to take risks, daring to try new things, and daring to push the limit a bit further."

When Men's Health caught up with Bonnet in Chamonix, France, during UTMB Mont-Blanc, one of the world's most prestigious trail-running events, he shared how his gear has evolved over the years. While he once obsessed over shaving every possible gram off his equipment, he's learned that lighter isn't always better, especially when it comes to performance.

We asked Bonnet to share the six pieces of gear he swears by, from his favorite trail-running shoes to a blister-prevention product.

As a Tudor ambassador, Bonnet has his pick of some seriously handsome watches, but the Ranger is his favorite. We're also big fans. Inspired by Tudor’s history of exploration, this rugged field watch features a stainless steel case, scratch-resistant sapphire crystal, and water resistance up to 100 meters, so it can take a licking. With multiple case sizes and strap options (stainless steel bracelet! Fabric strap! Rubber!), you can find one that fits your vibe, whether you're dressing up for dinner or heading outdoors.

Bonnet relies on Normatec compression boots after grueling races and long flights. The latest Elite model is completely wireless, with up to four hours of battery life, making it easy to squeeze in a leg massage whether you're at home or on the road. It also offers seven pressure settings to customize the intensity. A Men’s Health tester found the boots helped relieve his tired legs after a tough workout, and he even fell asleep during a 60-minute session.

Read more: Hyperice Normatec Elite Review

Before races, Bonnet puts on this anti-chafing cream. A blend of shea butter forms a thin, sweat-resistant barrier to help prevent blisters and friction mile after mile.

Bonnet loves these trail-running socks, which feature targeted cushioning in high-pressure areas like the heels and balls of the feet, plus moisture-wicking fabric to keep his feet dry mile after mile. They're also designed with extra support around the ankles to help lock the socks in place on uneven terrain.

As a Salomon-sponsored athlete, Bonnet is already running in the upcoming S/Lab Pulsar 5. "It is a mix between lightness and the performance of a road shoe," he says. Until that model hits shelves, the Pulsar 4 is the next best thing. It weighs just 9 ounces and features a dual-foam midsole, abrasion-resistant Matryx upper, and 3.5-millimeter rubber lugs for traction on rocky trails.

Bonnet uses an Insta360 camera to document his mountain adventures for Instagram. We're also fans of the brand, having awarded its GO Ultra a Men’s Health Tech Award in 2026. The latest X6 shoots sharp 8K video, with impressive image stabilization that keeps footage smooth even when you're shredding down a mountain. Its invisible selfie stick disappears from your footage for drone-like shots without needing someone else to film you.

#4727. My Health Anxiety Frustrates My Doctor; Now What?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

When the cardiologist frustratedly told me, “Look, I can’t tell you what every little thing you feel in your chest is,” I immediately felt invalidated, shamed, and guilty for having wasted his time. But I had been feeling discomfort in my chest for a while, and my primary care physician had referred me to a cardiologist as a precautionary measure. I was only following doctor’s orders. While the wisdom of hindsight tells me that I was experiencing anxiety, not a cardiac problem, I did not know it at the time, and I was relying on the cardiologist to give me some peace of mind, not to make me feel silly.

Many individuals who experience health anxiety have been in similar situations where a medical professional’s reaction has left them feeling worse rather than better at a medical appointment. There is a substantial body of research to support the idea that provider invalidation, dismissiveness, and lack of empathy are not only not uncommon but also make an already stressful situation for a health-anxious person even worse. A 2022 study concluded that “patients felt dismissed when they perceived that providers were rude or did not take action, provided poor information, did not believe patients, rushed the visit, or were uninformed" (Hildenbrand et al., 2022). A systematic review of 57 qualitative studies on the topic concluded that “due to the asymmetric physician-patient relationship, physicians should strive to treat patients with dignity and respect in order to alleviate the harmful effects of negative experiences” (Rocque & Leanza, 2015). Provider invalidation, such as that displayed by my cardiologist, is a serious problem for individuals who are already anxious about their health status.

So, what can a patient do if they find themselves in a clinical relationship with an invalidating provider? First, a recognition of a patient’s autonomy is necessary; patients must view the relationship from a place of equal footing and reframe the aforementioned “asymmetric physician-patient relationship.” Two human beings are in a medical office, both of whom deserve common courtesy. I like to remember that my medical appointments are about me, not the doctor. With this mindset, I can be less concerned about “annoying” or “bothering” my provider. My provider is there to provide services to me, and I have the freedom to ask what I need to ask, to express concern, or to seek reassurance. The doctor, in turn, has an obligation to treat my concerns respectfully and seriously, and to utilize a bedside manner that is appropriate and ethical.

We sometimes feel that once we have established a clinical relationship with a provider, we should maintain it even if we are unhappy with the service. Health-anxious people can feel a sense of obligation to their provider and a hesitation to question them or to seek out other opinions. If, however, you feel that your provider is not being appropriately attentive to your concerns or is behaving in an invalidating or dismissive manner, you have the freedom to change providers or seek a second opinion. Often, individuals feel that they are doing something “wrong” or “betraying” their doctor if they make a change, but the reality is that those who provide our services are not always the best match for us. And, particularly in medical matters, we have the autonomy and freedom to change course or go a different route to find a medical relationship that better aligns with our needs.

When it comes to your health, your medical care belongs to you. If, for instance, you wanted all your medical records, you are allowed to request them, and they must be provided by your provider—they belong to you by law. This sense of full autonomy is often forgotten by anxious patients, but reframing the experience of being a patient through a lens of autonomy and agency can be helpful in restoring a sense of self-governance. I am proud to say that my response to that cardiologist’s behavior was to seek a different one, and it was my self-determination that allowed me to recognize that I had no obligation to stay with an invalidating doctor and that it was my decision to go somewhere I would be treated more empathetically. Do not forget that, as a patient, you possess full autonomy.

Anxiety can rob us of our voice, make us feel that we should “hold it together,” and keep us from advocating for ourselves. But just because you have health anxiety does not mean you need to have a doctor who makes you feel worse. Our physical health is precious, and we all deserve to feel that it is being treated in a respectful and ethical way. Please remember that you deserve empathic care—even if you are an anxious patient. Many researchers agree that there is a “need for better support in developing empathic skills” among physicians (Gössi et al., 2025). In the meantime, you—the patient—can ensure that your medical care is reassuring, not triggering or invalidating.
